title: Diwali Noir Brings New York Fashion to BOOM for Festival of Lights
excerpt: ŌUSHQ and the CFDA filled BOOM at The Standard with brocades, jewel-toned silks and Indian designers on November 5 — and used the night to relaunch ŌUSHQ's platform.
body:
• ŌUSHQ and the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) hosted Diwali Noir at BOOM at The Standard, High Line, on November 5, 2026.
  • The evening was co-hosted by ŌUSHQ founder Jessel Taank and Prakti Beauty founder Pritika Swarup, in the event's second year.
  • Guests including Jenna Lyons, Rachel Roy, Bibhu Mohapatra and Sai De Silva followed an Indian-inspired dress code — brocades, embellished tailoring, jewel-toned silks and statement jewelry.
  • The party doubled as the relaunch of ŌUSHQ's e-commerce site and the debut of its editorial platform, ŌUSHQ ŌUTLINE.

New York's fashion calendar now has a Diwali fixture. ŌUSHQ and the Council of Fashion Designers of America returned to BOOM at The Standard, High Line, on Thursday, November 5, 2026, for Diwali Noir, an evening built around Indian craftsmanship and contemporary South Asian design, according to The Impression. It was the second edition of the party, following last year's inaugural CFDA–ŌUSHQ Diwali event.

The hosts and the room

The celebration was co-hosted by ŌUSHQ founder and chief executive Jessel Taank and Prakti Beauty founder and chief executive Pritika Swarup, alongside the CFDA's Marc Karimzadeh. The guest list crossed fashion, food and television: Jenna Lyons, Rachel Roy, Carly Cushnie, Bibhu Mohapatra, Michelle Ochs, Roopal Patel, Sai De Silva, Anjula Acharia, Ankur Jain, Jay Sean and chef Daniel Boulud were among those in the room, WWD's account of the evening reported.

"Some of the most exciting creative talent right now is coming out of India and the Middle East, and I've been very intentional about using my platform to bring more attention to it. I want these designers and creatives to be part of the global conversation, not just celebrated within our own communities."

— Jessel Taank, founder and CEO, ŌUSHQ

The looks

The dress code asked for Indian-inspired dressing read through a contemporary lens. Guests answered with brocades, embellished tailoring, jewel-toned silks, metallic accents and statement jewelry — festive codes, cut for a New York evening rather than a traditional celebration. Taank pointed to the designers she is watching: Dhruv Kapoor, who shows in Milan; Hussain Rehar from Lahore; Kanika Goyal; Shweta Kapur's 431-88; and Kaabia and Sasha Grewal's jewelry label Outhouse. Swarup said the modern dress code was deliberate — a push against the idea that Indian clothes are only traditional, and a demand that Indian creatives get credit inside everyday fashion culture.

More than a party

The evening also carried a business announcement: the relaunch of ŌUSHQ's multi-brand e-commerce website and the introduction of ŌUSHQ ŌUTLINE, an editorial destination for fashion, culture and emerging talent, led by editorial and content director Praachi Raniwala. Karimzadeh framed the partnership as cultural exchange, saying it recognizes "the influence of Indian craftsmanship on American fashion." Music came from Asad Khan, Raaginder (Mastaane) and Krish (TBOM); cocktails drew on Indian flavors alongside a Johnnie Walker Blue tasting, with Johnnie Walker Blue Label, Casamigos, Tri-State Cadillac, The Standard and FIJI Water supporting the event.

For Swarup, the meaning was simpler. "Growing up, Diwali was celebrated almost entirely at home, so seeing our traditions and culture embraced across New York today is deeply meaningful," she said. "At its core, Diwali is about the triumph of light over darkness."
